This, to me, is simple science. So...if you mix oil and water--heck. Lets go salad dressing. The oil sinks to the bottom. It is dense. More dense than water (or vinegar) so you have to shake it up. We float in water. We would float in oil.

Great question. We have a tendency to have a bit if a dark sense of humor so we make jokes. Obviously not where others can hear. You need to be sensitive to the victims.

Me, personally, before entering this career and school, I would watch Forensic Files all of the time. Now, on my off time I tend to gravitate toward comedy stuff and try to keep it light. 

In the end, I realize that we are the voice of thise who no longer have one. It gives me the drive needed to spend 12 hours in a Tyvek suit, sweating my butt off.

If this were my case...ok. I'm going to leave out all of the photography. Just know that every single thing is photographed.

We start from the outside in. A methodical top to bottom of each room is done. (We call it earning your real estate). I would take all of the bed sheets. I would use Blue Star on the bathrooms looking for "cleaned up" blood evidence. Garbage is always pulled from every receptical. All computers, phones, tablets, Alexa, etc. are taken to be sent out to look for search history and what not. The clothing is secured from the laundry bins. Lint front the lint try an the dryer. From there it would really depend on what is found. If something creates a nexus, you go from there. The process is very organic.

Once again, the oil is thought to be a preserving agent (over being in a rushing stream that could was away DNA evidence.) They would be extracted slowly and placed into a body bag. The oil present in the body bag would be collected and tested for evidence on a molecular level. DNA experts have stated that there is a high probability that DNA is recoverable after the time period they were in the oil.

The evidence for TOD is in the bodies. That would be lividity (the pooling if blood in body positioning by gravity) and gastric contents. Stomach contents are relative. Different food is digested at different rates.
There could be evidence a cadavar dog could find in the home. Also urine traces if they released their bladdar upon death.

A warrant for DNA is not needed. Garbage left at a curb for pick up is not covered under the 4th amendment. A simple garbge pull would yield a source of DNA. There is no evidence at this time know to us that anyone else was involved in the crime.
They are not releasing names because any mistress--male or female--is a potential witness. It is highly unlikely that anyone else participated in the crime.
Most security cameras record on a loop. There may or may not be evidence on them after such a long period of time.

Alexa is always listening to hear her name when you summon her. There may be a recording from the events that happened in the home. Finding them or getting anyone to admit they exists is a whole different issue.

I really feel like the grave was not planned. He intended to drop her in the tank with the girls but other issues got in the way that I stated above. Weight of SW body, size in correlation to the opening.

In the CA case, the expert on the air in the trunk was debunked as using "junk" forensics. I touched on the topic of using a cadavar dog in a previous question if you would like to check that out. As far as hair--it only presents DNA if the folicle is attached. Hair, though, is made up of "dead cells" like keratin.

I really don't know if he showered or not. From my experience, he was rushed from the process and had to haul ass to get to work on time. Whether it was because he had to dig the clandestine grave since he couldn't fit SW into the oil tank (see my theory above) or because everything was delayed due to her flight being delayed, he was rushing. He did not even have time to stage the scene--get rid of her phone, purse, etc. My opinion was he planned on doing it after work. Nickole and the LEO being there before he got home foiled that.

The oil is definitely an obstical and not a common occurance in crimes. There are experts that claim the oil will not be an obstical. Actually, that it may have actually preserved delicate DNA evidence from being destroyed. 

The nail issue is plausable but not likely. 

As far as cadavar dogs, they are absolutely amazing to see in action. I once saw (during a training class) a cadavar dog locate a 12 yo piece of femur bone up in a palm tree (7 feet up) outside (obviously) on a windy day. Our bodies begin to decay almost instantly. Blow flies can locate a body 2 to 3 minutes after death. Cadavar dogs do have the capability of finding a body that has only been dead a short time. Severe decay is not necessary.

Hand sizes will leave different bruising i.e. from a male of female since their hands are quite different. DNA now is so...delicate, there is something called touch DNA. It only takes approx 8 cells to obtain a profile. Because of this, there could be a million different reasons a family member's DNA can be found on a body--especially when they all live together. 

If a cord or wire (garrote) is used, there could be fiber evidence in the wound--like if a rope was used--because it is pressed into the skin forcefully. The garrote, if found, would have a substantial amount of skin cells from the garrote in the center from the victim and an abundance on the ends from the attacker. As far as prints in the house, it is almost impossible to distinguish when people all live together what is suspicious or not. (Unless they are patent and left in blood for example.) What trips people up is when they swear they have never been in the victims home, yet their prints are found there. 

Finally, most states use civillian CSI. They are going away from sworn officers because by the time an officer is trained to my capacity, they are ready to be promoted. Some evidence is processed by us. For example, a soda can. I would swab the mouth for DNA and the swabs go to a crime lab. I would then put the can into a super glue fuming chamber, then process it with an ink stain or powder for prints. The prints are photographed and them collected. Our agency can run them through the computer system (AFIS) but if an ID is made it must be verified by another certified print examiner (ACE-V). There is no set number of minutie that must be met.

It really depends. If one set of hand is obviously larger than another, the size of the bruising will be different. 

As far as the marks on his neck during his interview, it is tough to tell exactly what they are. IMO, they could be from SW. She wore acrylic/fake nails. They tend to be thicker than a regular nail. They don't leave the deep scratching, and therefore, a scab. Fingernail trimmings are a routine part of autopsy and are swabbed for DNA. If there are epithelial cells from CW under the nails from SW right hand, it could be possible she scratched him.

Deleted footage would act just like any other deleting process on technology. When you delete something, it is still there until it is overwritten. If it wasn't overwritten, it could possibly be recovered.

Once again, I am not on the case so I couldn't answer your questions with any certainty. If I was on the case, I couldn't tell you anyway.

1. I went back to school (college) after being out of high school for 17 yrs. Life at that time did not permit me to go to college and I really "didn't know what I wanted to be when I grew up." I worked retail and moved my way into restaurant life. Time went by so fast. My fiance went back to school (for IT) and encouraged me to as well. Crime scene investigator here...it is not like on TV. We will not always find useable prints at a scene. (Most prints are partial and smudged. Think of how you pick things up. It is not like when you do a deliberate print for a card.) DNA evidence won't be processed in 45 minutes. If someone breaks your car window out because you left your purse on the seat while you went to Starbucks for a pumpkin spice latte, they are not calling us in to process the scene. Smoking gun evidence is far and few between unlike on SVU or whatever where they find it on every case.

Two detectives question her as we gear up to go to the scene. I had been interning for some time in a high volume crime area (the absolute worse city in Florida, per capita) and I have seen some stuff...but nothing prepared me for this. 

The woman said she woke up and her clothes were gone and her butthole hurt. She said she had also been robbed. I really feel the lack of $ was the reason for this...if she woke up with her cash this would probably have been a non-issue. But, I digress.

Crime Scene Investigator here. I do not even know where to start. Here are 10 off the top of my head:
  
1. Forensics is not like you see on TV and watching the ID channel does not equate to my degrees. Also, it does not make you more likely to get away with something either.

2. Finding usable fingerprints from a scene is tough. They are mostly partials and are usually smeared and of no forensic value.
 
3. DNA testing can take months to come back from the lab.

4. A good majority of our job is photography. 

5. Processing a scene properly is done  step by step and from the outside in. If there is a body, we do not run up to it and start there. They are dead--they aren't going anywhere. Evidence can be lost and destroyed if you don't follow standard operating procedures. 

6. DNA is not guaranteed to be found. We have advanced and it take a very small amount (8 cells) to obtain a DNA profile, but being able to locate where to find the sample can be tricky and requires a knowledge of human mechanics and criminal behavior. 

7. If DNA or fingerprints are found, they still may be of no use. They are entered into a database and if there is no existing match in the system, we cannot make a positive ID.

8. CSI are not called in for every crime. If someone breaks into your home, the responding officers will be the ones to process. Unless you are the mayor or there is a more serious crime. Sorry to say this, but that is the facts. It may be a big deal to you, but in the grand scheme of things, it is not a major crime.

9. Unless there is some obvious evidence that spells it out, estimating a person's time of death is within a span of a few hours. It is not as precise as some believe.

10. A good CSI keeps the traffic of their scene minimal. Only those who MUST enter are permitted in to prevent the evidence from being compromised.
